metadata.title: HPSC FSO Unit 6 — Food Toxicology, Inherent Toxicants, Contaminants, Residues & Heavy Metals
metadata.option_format: Four substantive options (A–D); single best answer

source_coverage.plant_toxicants_and_antinutritional_fact: Legume toxicants, cyanogenic glycosides, favism, lectins, protease inhibitors, phytate, glycoalkaloids, glucosinolates, oxalates and argemone oil
source_coverage.marine_and_animal_biotoxins: Shellfish poisoning syndromes, sodium-channel toxins, ciguatoxin, tetrodotoxin and scombroid/histamine poisoning
source_coverage.heavy_metals: Lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic and tin
source_coverage.residues_and_risk_assessment: Organochlorines, organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids, veterinary residues, antimicrobial resistance, NOAEL, ADI and MRL
source_coverage.analysis_and_enforcement: Relevant screening/confirmatory methods and representative sampling workflow

exam_style.approach: HPSC-oriented practice: mechanism-to-syndrome matching, food/toxin pairings, numerical anchors, analytical test identification, statutory concepts, absolute-qualifier distinctions and high-yield trap contrasts.
exam_style.important_pattern_caveat: This is a technical-topic MCQ practice bank, not a prediction of the exact main-paper format. The revised HPSC FSO 2026 scheme reported for the 16 October 2026 notice describes the Screening Test as General Studies/Haryana GK and the Subject Knowledge Test as subjective/descriptive. Use these MCQs for technical recall and concept testing, and convert the explanations into descriptive SKT answers.
exam_style.screening_test_reported: 100 MCQs, 100 marks, 2 hours, English; five OMR options with the fifth for unattempted; one-fourth negative marking; minimum 25%; screening marks not counted in final merit.
exam_style.subject_knowledge_test_reported: 150 marks, 3 hours, subjective/descriptive, English; 35% qualifying; 87.5% final merit weightage; interview 12.5%.
exam_style.dates_reported: Screening Test 6 December 2026; Subject Knowledge Test 31 January 2027. Verify any later HPSC corrigendum.

source_limitations_and_cautions: The uploaded handout warns that statutory numerical limits may change by Gazette amendment and that its figures are representative values drawn from the 2011 Regulations and 2018–2020 harmonisation amendments.
Questions involving legal limits are restricted to values explicitly stated in the handout. Verify the latest notified commodity-specific table before using any figure as current law.
International values (Codex, JECFA, EU or other jurisdictions) must not be confused with Indian statutory limits.
No question claims that a practice question is guaranteed to appear in the examination.
metadata.source_exam_trap_compendium_coverage: The question set incorporates the handout's dedicated HPSC EXAM TRAP distinctions across plant toxicants, marine biotoxins, heavy metals, pesticide/veterinary residues and process contaminants.

detailed_explanations.explanation: Lathyrus sativus contains beta-N-oxalyl-L-alpha,beta-diaminopropionic acid (BOAA), also called ODAP. It is a glutamate analogue that produces excitotoxic injury in motor pathways and can cause irreversible spastic paraparesis.

The handout identifies BOAA as a structural analogue of glutamate and an agonist at AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors. Sustained sodium and calcium influx contributes to excitotoxicity and motor-neuron injury.

Neurolathyrism is a predominantly upper-motor-neuron syndrome. Spastic gait, hypertonia, exaggerated knee and ankle jerks, clonus and extensor plantar responses are typical; sensation and bladder function are usually spared.

Statements (i) and (ii) are correct: khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) contains BOAA/ODAP, which acts as an AMPA-type glutamate receptor agonist. Statement (iii) is incorrect because dry roasting removes little or no ODAP; wet processing followed by discarding the water is required.

The handout distinguishes neurolathyrism due to BOAA in Lathyrus sativus from osteolathyrism due to beta-aminopropionitrile in Lathyrus odoratus. The latter interferes with lysyl oxidase and collagen cross-linking.

Linamarin is the major cyanogenic glycoside in cassava; lotaustralin is present in smaller amounts. Amygdalin is associated with bitter almonds and stone-fruit kernels, while dhurrin occurs in sorghum.
Amygdalin is a cyanogenic glycoside found in bitter almonds and apricot and related kernels. Hydrolysis releases benzaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide and two glucose units.

Cyanide binds ferric iron in cytochrome c oxidase, stopping electron transfer to oxygen and oxidative phosphorylation. Oxygen may remain in arterial blood, but tissues cannot utilise it, producing histotoxic hypoxia and lactic acidosis.

All three statements are correct. Linamarin is the principal cyanogenic glycoside of cassava, amygdalin occurs in bitter almonds and stone-fruit kernels, and dhurrin occurs in sorghum, especially young shoots.

Disruption of the plant tissue compartments permits endogenous linamarase to hydrolyse linamarin and release cyanohydrin/HCN. Boiling intact chunks first can denature the enzyme before adequate hydrolysis occurs.

G6PD supplies NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway in mature red cells. NADPH is required to regenerate reduced glutathione, which protects haemoglobin and the red-cell membrane against oxidant stress from faba-bean metabolites.

Vicine and convicine are hydrolysed to divicine and isouramil. These unstable aglycones generate reactive oxygen species and oxidise glutathione, precipitating haemoglobin as Heinz bodies and causing haemolysis in susceptible G6PD-deficient individuals.

Favism is not an allergy or cyanide poisoning. It is triggered by oxidant metabolites of faba beans in people with G6PD deficiency; the handout notes that vicine and convicine are heat-stable, so ordinary cooking does not reliably prevent it.

Red kidney beans contain the lectin phytohaemagglutinin. The handout reports high haemagglutinating activity in raw beans and notes that even a small number of inadequately cooked beans can cause acute gastrointestinal illness.
PHA is a protein denatured by adequate moist heat at boiling temperature. The handout warns that sub-boiling slow-cooker temperatures may increase extractability/activity; dry heat is unreliable.

The handout specifically flags heating at about 70–80°C as unsafe because it may increase extractability and measured haemagglutinating activity. Proper vigorous boiling or pressure cooking is the reliable control described.

Statements (i) and (ii) are correct. Vicine and convicine are hydrolysed to oxidant aglycones, and G6PD-deficient red cells have limited NADPH-dependent glutathione regeneration. Statement (iii) is false because these glycosides are heat-stable.

Inhibition of luminal trypsin reduces feedback that normally limits CCK-releasing signals. Increased CCK chronically stimulates pancreatic acinar cells, increasing digestive-enzyme secretion and, particularly in rodents, causing hypertrophy/hyperplasia.

The handout identifies a trypsin inhibitor activity assay using benzoyl-DL-arginine-p-nitroanilide (BAPNA) substrate. Urease activity is an indirect heat-treatment indicator because urease and trypsin inhibitors have similar heat sensitivity.
Phytic acid is myo-inositol 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexakis(dihydrogen phosphate), commonly called IP6. Its multiple negatively charged phosphate groups bind mineral cations and reduce their bioavailability.
The handout ranks zinc as the most affected mineral, followed by iron, then calcium and magnesium. Phytate forms poorly soluble complexes at intestinal pH, reducing mineral absorption.

Germination activates/synthesises plant phytase, while fermentation provides microbial phytase and favourable acidic conditions. Ordinary cooking alone produces relatively little reduction because phytate is heat-stable.
The handout gives a phytate-to-zinc molar ratio above 15 as a marker of markedly impaired zinc absorption. This is a nutritional bioavailability indicator, not a direct acute-poisoning threshold.

Statements (i) and (ii) are correct. The 200 mg/kg value is for total glycoalkaloids (solanine plus chaconine), not a separate allowance for each. Statement (iii) is false because these compounds are relatively heat-stable and are little changed by ordinary boiling.
The handout gives 200 mg/kg fresh tuber as the total glycoalkaloid ceiling for solanine plus chaconine. It is not a separate 200 mg/kg allowance for each compound.

Greening reflects chlorophyll formation, but the same light exposure can stimulate glycoalkaloid synthesis. Chlorophyll is not the toxin; green, sprouted, bitter or damaged tubers should be discarded or carefully excluded.

The handout notes that glycoalkaloids are relatively heat-stable and are little changed by boiling, baking or microwaving. Peeling and removal of sprouts/eyes reduce exposure, while visibly green or bitter tubers should be discarded.
Progoitrin has a 2-hydroxy side chain and can cyclise to goitrin (5-vinyl-oxazolidine-2-thione). Sinigrin instead produces allyl isothiocyanate, associated with mustard pungency.

Goitrin and related thiones inhibit thyroid peroxidase, interfering with iodination of tyrosyl residues and coupling reactions. Unlike thiocyanate-mediated inhibition of iodide uptake, this mechanism is not overcome simply by increasing iodine intake.

Thiocyanate competes with iodide at the thyroid sodium–iodide symporter. The handout contrasts this with goitrin's inhibition of thyroid peroxidase and notes that adequate iodine can help overcome the uptake competition.
Progoitrin is the glucosinolate precursor of goitrin. Sinigrin gives allyl isothiocyanate, so assigning goitrin to sinigrin is a specific exam trap.

Colocasia contains insoluble calcium oxalate crystals called raphides. Needle-like crystals irritate and pierce oral mucosa, producing burning, itching and oedema; adequate cooking and acidic ingredients can reduce acridity.

All three statements are correct. The nitric acid (Hofmann) test is a screening test with lower sensitivity; paper chromatography is a highly sensitive confirmatory method. Sanguinarine is the key toxic alkaloid in argemone oil.

The handout highlights that calcium in spinach is substantially associated with oxalate, lowering its bioavailability. Calcium-rich foods consumed with an oxalate-rich meal can bind oxalate in the intestinal lumen.
Argemone mexicana seeds resemble mustard seeds and can contaminate mustard seed lots. Its oil contains sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine, which are associated with epidemic dropsy.

Argemone oil contains benzophenanthridine alkaloids, especially sanguinarine and its reduced form dihydrosanguinarine. Sanguinarine is associated with vascular endothelial effects and increased capillary permeability.

The nitric acid test produces a reddish-brown to orange-red colour in the acid layer and detects approximately 0.25% argemone oil and above. Paper chromatography is the more sensitive confirmatory test.
Paper chromatography separates sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine from the oil matrix and is described as detecting as low as 0.0001%. The nitric acid test is a less sensitive screening test.
PSP is caused by saxitoxin and related analogues, commonly produced by dinoflagellates such as Alexandrium. Filter-feeding shellfish can concentrate the toxin.
Saxitoxin plugs the outer pore (site 1) of voltage-gated sodium channels and prevents sodium entry. Nerve conduction fails, causing paraesthesia, weakness and potentially respiratory paralysis.

The handout gives 80 micrograms saxitoxin equivalents per 100 g shellfish meat, equivalent to 0.8 mg/kg. It is a high-yield numerical anchor and should be checked against the current applicable notification before regulatory use.
Domoic acid, the ASP toxin, is associated with diatoms of the genus Pseudo-nitzschia. The handout contrasts this with PSP, DSP and NSP, which are linked to dinoflagellates.

All three statements are correct. Saxitoxin causes PSP, domoic acid from Pseudo-nitzschia diatoms causes ASP, and okadaic acid/dinophysistoxins cause DSP through inhibition of serine/threonine protein phosphatases.

Okadaic acid and dinophysistoxins inhibit serine/threonine protein phosphatases, particularly PP2A and also PP1. Hyperphosphorylation disrupts epithelial barrier and transport functions, producing diarrhoea.

DSP typically presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, especially profuse diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. It is generally self-limiting, unlike the potentially life-threatening respiratory paralysis of PSP.
Karenia brevis is the dinoflagellate associated with brevetoxins and NSP. The handout also notes aerosolised toxin in sea spray during blooms as a cause of respiratory irritation.

Brevetoxins bind site 5 and shift channel activation while preventing normal inactivation. Persistent sodium influx produces membrane depolarisation and repetitive firing, the opposite functional outcome to site-1 blockers.
Saxitoxin and tetrodotoxin block the sodium-channel pore at site 1. Brevetoxin and ciguatoxin bind site 5 and promote channel opening; this distinction is repeatedly flagged in the handout.
Tetrodotoxin is associated with bacterial symbionts and accumulation in pufferfish. It blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, similar in mechanism to saxitoxin, but has a different source association.

Ciguatoxin enters reef fish through the marine food chain, with benthic dinoflagellates as the original source. It is heat-stable and can cause gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms, including temperature-reversal sensations.

Scombroid poisoning results when bacteria convert histidine in susceptible fish to histamine during temperature abuse. It can mimic allergy but is a pseudo-allergic intoxication and can affect non-allergic individuals.
Rapid chilling suppresses bacterial growth and histidine decarboxylase activity. Histamine is heat-stable, so cooking, canning or reheating does not reliably remove histamine already formed.
Histamine is a heat-stable preformed chemical hazard. It is not reliably removed by cooking or canning and scombroid poisoning is not an IgE-mediated allergy.

Lead interferes with haem synthesis by inhibiting delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) and ferrochelatase. This can cause anaemia and accumulation of haem precursors despite adequate iron stores.

Itai-itai disease occurred in the Jinzu River basin of Toyama, Japan, and was linked to cadmium-contaminated irrigation water and rice. Renal tubular dysfunction and bone demineralisation/osteomalacia were characteristic.

All three are correct as the disease–toxicant associations summarised in the handout. Itai-itai is linked to cadmium, Minamata to methylmercury, and blackfoot disease to chronic arsenic exposure in Taiwan.

Minamata disease was caused by methylmercury discharged into Minamata Bay and bioaccumulated in fish and shellfish. Methylmercury is neurotoxic and crosses the placenta, making foetal exposure particularly harmful.
In aquatic systems, microorganisms can methylate inorganic mercury. Methylmercury accumulates in organisms and biomagnifies up the food chain, so large predatory fish may carry higher concentrations.

The handout lists paraesthesia of lips and fingers, constriction of visual fields, cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, deafness and tremor in adult methylmercury poisoning. Foetal exposure can cause severe developmental neurological injury.

Methylmercury binds strongly to proteins such as cysteine-containing compounds and is efficiently absorbed from fish. It crosses the blood–brain and placental barriers and biomagnifies in aquatic food chains.

The handout describes rice uptake of arsenite through silicon transporters Lsi1 and Lsi2. Anaerobic paddy conditions favour mobile As(III), and bran/husk tend to contain more arsenic than polished rice.

Arsenite binds paired sulphydryl groups, including those in dihydrolipoamide-dependent enzyme complexes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase. This impairs entry of pyruvate into the citric acid cycle and reduces ATP generation.

Chronic arsenic exposure can cause pigmentary changes, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, neuropathy and cancers including skin, lung and bladder cancer. Arsenic-contaminated groundwater is a major public-health exposure route.

Arsenic-rich alluvial aquifers affect parts of West Bengal and adjoining areas including Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Assam and Jharkhand. The handout emphasises shallow tube wells tapping geogenic arsenic-rich aquifers.
Acidic foods promote detinning, and nitrate and dissolved oxygen can further accelerate electrochemical dissolution. Internal can lacquering, oxygen exclusion and cool storage are control measures.
The handout identifies nitrate as a major accelerator, acting as a cathodic depolariser, alongside acidity and dissolved oxygen. The combination increases dissolution of tin from the can coating.

The handout gives 250 mg/kg for canned foods and 150 mg/kg for canned beverages. It notes that inorganic tin is poorly absorbed and primarily causes local gastrointestinal irritation at high concentrations.

Statements (i) and (ii) are correct. ADI is a health-based daily intake estimate derived from NOAEL divided by an uncertainty factor; MRL is a pesticide–commodity residue limit. Statement (iii) is false because they measure different things.

NOAEL is the highest tested exposure level at which no adverse effect is observed under the conditions of the study. It is used as a starting point in deriving health-based guidance values such as ADI.
ADI is derived by dividing the NOAEL by the uncertainty/safety factor: 2.5 ÷ 100 = 0.025 mg/kg body weight/day. Multiplying by 100 is the classic reversal trap.

A conventional uncertainty factor of 100 is often represented as 10 for extrapolation from animals to humans multiplied by 10 for variability among humans. It is an uncertainty factor, not a multiplier applied to the NOAEL.

MRLs are pesticide–commodity-specific trading/compliance limits, generally based on supervised residue trials under good agricultural practice and checked against dietary exposure. ADI is a health-based estimate of daily intake per body weight, so the two are not interchangeable.

ADI is expressed as an amount per kilogram body weight per day and is intended for lifetime daily exposure. MRL is expressed as residue concentration in a particular commodity and reflects authorised use and residue data.
Organochlorines are chemically stable and lipophilic, so they persist and accumulate in adipose tissue and may biomagnify. Their residues can enter dairy fat and breast milk.

The handout describes DDT as prolonging the open state of voltage-gated sodium channels, causing repetitive neuronal firing, tremor and convulsions. Cyclodienes and lindane are contrasted as GABA-A chloride-channel antagonists.

Organophosphates (often bioactivated from P=S to P=O oxons) phosphorylate the serine hydroxyl at the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase. The enzyme may undergo ageing, making reactivation more difficult.

Acetylcholinesterase inhibition causes acetylcholine accumulation at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. The resulting syndrome includes secretions, bronchospasm, miosis, bradycardia, fasciculations, weakness and potentially respiratory failure.

Pralidoxime can reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase if administered before the enzyme–organophosphate complex ages. Atropine treats muscarinic manifestations; pralidoxime is not routinely indicated for carbamate poisoning.

Carbamates reversibly carbamylate acetylcholinesterase and the enzyme generally recovers spontaneously within minutes to hours. This is why pralidoxime is not generally recommended as a routine treatment for carbamate poisoning.
Synthetic pyrethroids act on voltage-gated sodium channels. In humans, the handout identifies paraesthesia of exposed skin as a common effect, while severe exposure may cause tremor or seizures.
The handout lists red for extremely toxic, yellow for highly toxic, blue for moderately toxic and green for slightly toxic. Questions often test the order and exact pairing.

Statements (i) and (ii) are correct. Organophosphates can cause enzyme ageing after phosphorylation, whereas carbamate inhibition is generally reversible. Statement (iii) is false; pralidoxime is not routinely recommended for carbamate poisoning.

The handout identifies chloramphenicol as a prohibited residue, not a substance with an ordinary positive MRL. Its association with aplastic anaemia is the key reason for the zero-tolerance exam distinction.
Microbial inhibition tests such as Delvotest and Charm can screen for antimicrobial residues. Positive screens require appropriate confirmatory analysis, for example LC–MS/MS.

LC–MS/MS is a powerful confirmatory technique for veterinary drug residues because it combines chromatographic separation with selective mass transitions. Screening and confirmation should not be confused.
Antibiotic exposure creates selection pressure that favours resistant organisms. Resistance can spread through mutation or acquisition and transfer of resistance genes, including plasmid-borne genes.
PAHs form during incomplete combustion and pyrolysis, particularly when fat drips onto flames and smoke deposits on food. Direct charring and high-temperature smoking can increase contamination.
Benzo[a]pyrene is a five-ring PAH used as a marker compound. The handout also describes the PAH4 group used in some regulatory frameworks.
Benzo[a]pyrene is metabolically activated through cytochrome P450 and epoxide hydrolase pathways to BPDE. BPDE is the ultimate carcinogenic epoxide that can form DNA adducts.

Indirect smoking, lower temperatures, filtered/liquid smoke and avoiding fat dripping onto flames reduce PAH formation and deposition. Removing charred portions and limiting direct flame contact are additional mitigation measures.

Acrylamide forms mainly through Maillard chemistry involving free asparagine and reducing sugars in low-moisture foods heated above roughly 120°C. Potato chips, fries, toasted bread and roasted coffee are examples.

All three are correct. PAHs are associated with combustion/pyrolysis and smoke deposition; acrylamide forms mainly from asparagine and reducing sugars during high-temperature low-moisture processing; ethyl carbamate can form when urea reacts with ethanol.
Cytochrome P450 2E1 metabolises acrylamide to glycidamide, an epoxide that can form DNA adducts. Acrylamide itself is also associated with peripheral neurotoxicity in occupational exposure.

The handout notes that cold storage can cause cold sweetening, increasing reducing sugars in potatoes. More reducing sugar can react with free asparagine during frying and increase acrylamide formation.

One major route described is urea released during arginine metabolism reacting with ethanol to form ethyl carbamate. Heat and storage time can accelerate formation; citrulline may provide another precursor in some fermentations.
The handout lists low-urea yeast strains and acid urease addition as mitigation strategies. Limiting precursor formation and controlling processing/storage conditions can reduce ethyl carbamate.

The handout lists atomic absorption spectrometry and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry for metals. These instrumental methods support quantitative determination after suitable sample digestion and quality control.
QuEChERS is a widely used sample-preparation approach for pesticide residue analysis. The handout links it to subsequent GC- or LC-based instrumental analysis, including tandem mass spectrometry.

Pesticides vary in volatility and polarity, so GC–MS/MS and LC–MS/MS are both used depending on the analyte. The handout emphasises screening followed by confirmatory analysis and comparison with current commodity-specific limits.

The handout repeatedly warns that heavy-metal limits are commodity-specific. The correct legal comparison requires identifying the food category, metal species where relevant, units and latest applicable notification.
